views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current tariff posture and negotiate firmly from leverage, but do not escalate further at this juncture. The resumed talks post-G20 Osaka represent the best channel for extracting structural concessions from China. Use existing tariffs and the Huawei Entity List as bargaining chips while avoiding the $300B tariff expansion that would directly hit US consumers in an election year.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate and rising, driven by three factors. First, the trade war is imposing real costs on the US economy: the Fed's July 2019 report flagged that tariffs have had a 'material' impact on manufacturing growth (Federal Reserve semi-annual report to Congress, July 5, 2019); Dallas Fed surveys show over half of manufacturers reporting higher input costs and cutting capex (Dallas Fed speech, June 24, 2019); and economists estimate a 0.1-0.3% GDP drag (CBO, IMF, FactCheck.org analysis, May 2019). Second, US farmers are under severe stress — soybean exports to China collapsed from $14B in 2017 to near zero after China's 25% retaliatory tariff, prices fell from $10.89 to $8.68/bushel, and the USDA had to deploy a $16B bailout (USDA, May 23, 2019; American Soybean Association testimony, June 19, 2019). Third, the $300B tariff threat on remaining Chinese consumer goods would cost the average American household $831/year (NY Fed estimate) and risk broad consumer price increases heading into 2020.

However, the US holds significant leverage. China's GDP just hit a 27-year low at 6.2% in Q2 (National Bureau of Statistics, July 15, 2019), exports to the US are down 8.1% year-on-year, and total imports are down 7.3%. The Huawei Entity List action (May 16, 2019) is a powerful pressure point — Google suspended Android access, major chip suppliers paused sales, and SoftBank chose Nokia/Ericsson for 5G over Huawei. China's retaliatory tools (rare earth threats, unreliable entity list) are more limited in immediate economic impact. The G20 Osaka truce (June 29, 2019) bought time but produced no firm commitments from either side — Chinese officials have been clear they made no specific agricultural purchase promises, and Huawei remains effectively blacklisted despite Trump's vague easing signals.

The action_score of -0.15 reflects a negotiate posture tilted slightly toward maintaining pressure. Escalation (the $300B tariff list) would be counterproductive: it would hit US consumers directly, further damage farm-belt political support, and invite Chinese retaliation before talks have had a chance to produce results. But full de-escalation or concession would surrender the leverage that is currently working — China's economic slowdown gives the US genuine bargaining power. The right move is to hold tariffs at current levels, keep Huawei on the Entity List as a chip, and push the resumed negotiations toward structural IP protections, forced tech transfer reform, and enforceable purchase commitments. If talks stall again after a reasonable window, escalation remains available; premature escalation would squander leverage rather than increase it.
key_factors: China GDP at 27-year low (6.2% Q2 2019) — US leverage is real but fragile
US manufacturing surveys deteriorating; Fed flagged 'material' tariff impact on manufacturing
Farm sector under severe stress: $16B bailout needed, soybean exports to China collapsed
Huawei Entity List (May 16) is powerful leverage — Google/supplier cutoff, but policy signal muddled by Trump's G20 easing comments
G20 Osaka truce (June 29) resumed talks but no firm commitments from either side
Threat of $300B tariff expansion would directly hit US consumers — $831/household cost
China retaliatory tools (rare earths, unreliable entity list) less immediately damaging than US tariffs
Fed signaling rate cuts, suggesting economic softening that tariff escalation could worsen

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Osaka: Trump and Xi agree to resume talks. Existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs 'for the time being.'
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.

The tariffs imposed by the United States and some of its trading partners, combined with the uncertainty around trade policy were likely 'material' in the sharp slowdown in global manufacturing growth last year, the Fed said.
China's exports fell 1.3% year-on-year for the first half in dollar terms, while imports dropped 7.3%. China's exports to the United States decreased 8.1% for the first six months of 2019.
President Trump authorized USDA to provide up to $16 billion in programs, in line with the estimated impacts of unjustified retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural goods.
Sources familiar with the talks and China trade watchers in Washington say the summit did little to clear the path for top negotiators to resolve an impasse.
